la:noun:congressus.html:
congressus, ūs, m.
congredior
,
a coming or going together, in a friendly or hostile manner (class. in prose and poetry).
A friendly meeting, a social assembly, conference, conversation, etc.: omnes congressum tuum fugiunt,; ; : si quis congressus fuerit mihi cum Caesare,; ; ; ; et saep.—In plur., ; ; ; ; ; —Also of the companionship of animals, ; .—
Pregn., a close union, combination (very rare): materiaï,; cf.: duriorum (consonantium) inter se,.— In plur., .—Hence, carnal union, copulation: feminarum,; cf. congressio, I. B.—
A hostile encounter, a contest, fight, : cum his navibus nostrae classi ejusmodi congressus erat, ut, etc.,; : magnam cladem in congressu facere,; ; ; ; —Also of judicial contests, .

la:verb:congredior.gloss: to go, come or meet with someone, approach; visit, accost, address
senses: to go, come or meet with someone, approach; visit, accost, address
la:verb:congredior.html:
con-grĕdĭor, gressus, 3, v. dep.
gradior
,
to go, come, or meet with one, esp. with the access. idea of intention, in a friendly or hostile sense (class. in prose and poetry); constr. with cum (contra, etc.), the acc., dat., or absol.
In a friendly sense, to visit, accost, address, meet with.
With cum: insinuatus in familiaritatem adulescentis et cum eo saepe congressus,: luna tum congrediens cum sole, tum digrediens,: perquirere ubi sit congressus cum servis Caelius,: qui cum Caesare in itinere congressi ... orabant,.—
With acc.: hunc,; . 1, 19.—
Absol., ; ; ; ; ; ; : in eo loco ut congrederentur convenit,; ; : in Macedoniā congrediemur, Brut. ap. : congressa primordia rerum,; ; .—
In a hostile sense, to fight, contend, engage. etc. (most freq. in the historians).
With cum: cum hostibus,: saepenumero cum his,; ; ; ; ; .— *
With contra: contra ipsum Caesarem est congressus armatus,.—*
With adversus, .—*
With inter se, .—(ε) With dat. (poet. or in post-Aug. prose): infelix puer atque impar congressus Achilli,; ; : quippe armato congredi nudum dementia videbatur,; .—

(ζ) Absol.: locus ad insidias ille, ubi congressi sunt, utri fuerit aptior,: Aedui quoniam armis congressi ac superati essent,; so fin.; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : totis viribus,: in congrediendis hostibus, (cf. id. § 9: in congressibus proeliorum).—

Transf., of contention in words, specif. of judic. strife (almost confined to Cic. and Quint.): tecum luctari et congredi,; so : cum Academico et eodem rhetore,; pr.; Cod. 7, 56, 3.—
With abstract subjects: quasi ad repugnandum congressa defensio,; cf. : oratio aequo congressa campo,.

la:adj:congiarius.html:
congĭārĭus, a, um, adj.
congius
,
pertaining to a congius, holding a congius.
As adj. rare: vinum, given by measure, Cato ap. Mai: cadi, Varr. ap. .—But very freq. subst.,
congĭārĭum, ii, n.
(Sc. vas.) A vessel that holds a congius, ; cf. .—
(Sc. donum.) A gift divided among the people of the measure of a congius; cf. Quint. 6, 3, 52. Orig. this present was in food; as in oil, (v. congius); in salt,; in wine,. Afterwards congiarium was also used for a largess in money of undefined amount; divided among the soldiers, ; ; ; ; among the people, ; ; ; ; ; ; , in which sense post-Aug. authors contrast it with the donativum of the soldiers, ; ; ; ; or among private friends, Cael. ap. ; ; ; Quint. l. l.; ; ; ; cf. Dict. of Antiq.: in hunc maxime quod multa congiaria habuerat, favor populi se inclinabat,because he had made many distributions, (v. Drak. ad h. l.); so .—
Transf., in gen., a gift, present, ; cf. .

la:noun:congiarium.gloss: A vessel that holds a congius
senses: A vessel that holds a congius
A gift (of that measure) distributed to the people

la:verb:congero.gloss: to bring together; to collect or accumulate
senses: to bring together; to collect or accumulate
la:verb:congero.html:
con-gĕro, gessi, gestum, 3,
v. a., to bear, carry, or bring together, to collect; to prepare, to make, build, heap up, etc. (class. and freq.).
Lit.
With acc.: undique, quod idoneum ad muniendum putarent,: congestis undique saccis,: cetera aedificanti utilia,: caedi arbores et saxa congeri jubet,: alimenta undique,: frondem,: virgulta arida,: robora,: arma,: tura,; cf.: turea dona,: epulas alicui,: cibaria sibi,: viaticum,: divitias sibi fulvo auro,: opes,: congestoque avidum pinguescere corpore corpus,: nemus,i. e. wood,; cf. silvas,: siccā congestā pulvere barbā,terram,; cf. : oscula congerimus properata,to join, add one to another, (18), 113.—
With acc., and a designation of place to, at, or in which, etc., any thing is brought or heaped up: hasce herbas in suum alvum,; cf. : in cellulam patris penum omnem congerebam,: laticem in vas,; cf. : Midae dormienti formicae in os tritici grana congesserunt,; cf.: in os pueri,: excrementa in unum locum,; ; : scuta illi (sc. virgini) pro aureis donis congesta,; cf. : sestertium millies in culinam,to expend,: huc amnes vastos congerit tellus,: Pindo congestus Athos,: uni (digito anulos),: humum corbulae,.—
In partic.
Of weapons, missiles, etc., to throw in great numbers, accumulate, shower, etc.: lanceas,: saxa in caput alicujus,: in ipsum Porum tela,: congestis telis,.—Hence, poet.: ictus alicui,: plagas mortuo,.—
To make, build, construct, etc., by bringing or heaping together: Echinades insulae ab Acheloo amne congestae,: aram sepulcri arboribus,: oppida manu,: pauperis et tuguri congestum caespite culmen,.—So of birds, insects, etc.: lucifugis congesta cubilia blattis,: nidum,; and absol. notavi Ipse locum aëriae quo congessere palumbes (sc. nidum), ; (cf. the full expression: in nervom ille hodie nidamenta congeret,): apes in alvearium congesserant, Cic. Oecon. Fragm. ap. P.: rape, congere, aufer,.—
Trop.
In discourse, to bring, take, or comprise together, to compile (freq. in Quint.): operarios omnes,: dicta,; cf. : argumenta (opp. dissolvere),: vana (maledicta),: undique nomina plurimorum poëtarum,: orationem dierum ac noctium studio,; cf.: orationem ex diversis,: figuras,: ζωὴ καὶ ψυχή lascivum congeris usque, i. e. you repeat, .—With in: ut te eripias ex eā, quam ego congessi in hunc sermonem, turbā patronorum,; so ; ; ; 10, 5, 23.—
To put something upon one in a hostile or friendly manner, to accumulate, heap upon, to impart, ascribe to, to impute, attribute to; constr. class. with ad or in; post-Aug. also with dat. pers.: ad quem di

atque homines omnia ornamenta congessissent, : ne plus aequo quid in amicitiam congeratur,: ingentia beneficia in aliquem,; : congerere juveni consulatus, triumphos,; cf.: ambitiosae majestati quicquid potuimus titulorum congessimus,; ; : mortuo laudes congessit,: mala alicui,: μέλι μου, ψυχή μου congeris usque, : spes omnis in unum Te mea congesta est,: in unum omnia,; cf.: iis nihil, quo expleri possit eorum meritum, tributurum populum Romanum, si omnia simul congesserit, Brut. ap. .—Esp., of crimes, etc.: maledicta in aliquem,; cf.: congestis probris,: quae (crimina) postea sunt in eum congesta,: causas alicujus rei in aliquem,.— Hence, *congestus, a, um, P. a., lit. brought together; hence, in pregn. signif., pressed together, thick: gobio congestior alvo,.—* Adv.: congestē, briefly, summarily: haec breviter et congeste,

la:verb:congemo.gloss: to sigh or groan deeply (heave a sigh)
senses: to sigh or groan deeply (heave a sigh)
la:verb:congemo.html:
con-gĕmo, ŭi, 3, v. n. and a.
Neutr., to sigh or groan deeply or loudly, to heave a sigh.
Prop. (rare but class.): congemuit senatus frequens, * ; * .—
Transf., poet., of trees cut down: supremum congemuit, * .—
Act., to deplore, lament, bewail: quid mortem congemis ac fles? * : positum feretro congemuere,.

la:verb:congemino.html:
con-gĕmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. a., to double, redouble, repeat, reduplicate (poet.): nunc si pateram patera peperit, omnes congeminavimus,i. e. have produced our like, doubled ourselves,: L (litteram),: crebros ictus ensibus,; in the same sense, securim,: suspiria rauco fremitu,: paeana,: vocem,; .

la:verb:congruo.gloss: to come, unite, combine, run or meet together with someone
senses: to come, unite, combine, run or meet together with someone
to coincide or correspond with someone or something; agree with, be suited; accord, suit, fit
la:verb:congruo.html:
congrŭo, ŭi, 3 (
inf. pres. congruēre, ), v. n.
etym. dub.; cf. Corss. Beitr. 457
, to run, come, or meet together with something.
Prop. (rare; mostly post-Aug.): guttae inter se congruunt et confunduntur,: arcem nata petit, quo jam manus horrida matrum Congruerat,; ; of the stars: sidera meantia cum sole aut congruentia, § 191; cf. (cf. , II. B. infra).— Hence also of the calendar dates, fixed in accordance with the stars: ut vicesimo anno ad metam eandem solis, unde orsi essent, dies cóngruerent,.—Far more freq. and class. in prose and poetry,
Trop., to coincide or correspond with a person or thing, in substance, in feeling, or in time, to be suited or adapted to, to agree with, accord, suit, fit.
To be suited or fitted to, to agree with (in substance), to correspond; constr. with cum, inter se, the dat., or absol.
With cum: illa congruere et cohaerere cum causā,; so ; ; ; : cum virtute congruere semper, .—
With inter se: ut corporis temperatio, cum ea congruunt inter se, e quibus constamus, sanitas: sic animi dicitur, cum ejus judicia opinionesque concordant,: cum multae causae ... inter se congruere videntur,; ; ; .—Somewhat diff.: fidem auxere captivi eo maxime, quod sermo inter omnes congruebat (for sermones omnium inter se congruebant),agreed, was congruous,.—
With dat.: quibus (principiis) congruere debent quae sequuntur,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : non omni causae nec auditori neque personae neque tempori congruere orationis unum genus, is suitable, fit, = convenire, ; ; .—Impers.: Canidius timidius decessit quam professioni ejus congruebat,; .—
Absol.: quemadmodum congruit, ut simul et affirmes, te assiduis occupationibus impediri, et scripta nostra desideres?is it consistent?; cf. : res prout congruunt aut repugnant,; so ; ; ; : adversus Latinos bellandum erat, lingua, moribus, etc., congruentes,.—
To agree (in feeling, opinion, etc.): illi inter se congruunt concorditer,; : mulier mulieri magis congruit,; : linguā, moribus, armorum genere institutis ante omnia militaribus congruentes,: ecce autem similia omnia: omnes congruunt: unum cognoris, omnes noris,: de re unā solum dissident de ceteris mirifice congruunt,: vereor ne natura ... animos quoque dederit corporum doloribus congruentis,sympathizing with, sharing in, affected by,; cf.: sidera innumerabilia caelo inhaerentia cum ejus ipsius motu congruere, Tischer ad loc.—Rarely with in and acc.: Bruttiis non societate magis Punicā quam suopte ingenio congruentibus in eum morem, Weissenb. ad loc.; cf.: omniumque in unum sententiae congruebant,; : omnes eae res in unum congruentes ... damnationem faciebant,.—
To come together, agree, meet, coincide (in time): suos dies mensisque congruere volunt cum solis lunaeque ratione,: tempus ad id ipsum congruere,; so with ad, : cum temporum ratio vix congruat,: forte congruerat, ut Clodii Macri et Fonteii Capitonis caedes nuntiarentur,it happened at the same time,: in idem artati temporis,; ; .—Hence, congrŭens, entis, P. a. (acc. to II.).
Agreeing, fit, appropriate, suitable, consistent, congruous.
With cum: vita cum disciplinā,; ; : Aristoteles et Theophrastus, cum illis re congruentes, genere docendi paulum differentes,.—
With dat.: congruens actio menti,; ; ; ; .—Comp.: quid congruentius Deo?.—
Absol.: genus dicendi aptum et congruens,; : actio vocis, vultūs et gestūs,: oratio verbis discrepans, sententiis congruens,: cum haec duo pro congruentibus sumunt, tam vehementer repugnantia,.—Hence,
Congruens est or videtur, = convenit, it is (seems) fit, proper, meet (post-Aug. and rare); with acc. and inf.: congruens erat, eandem immunitatem parentes obtinere,: congruentius est, Cod. 8, 47, 4.—In sup.: congruentissimum est, animam puniri,.—With inf.: congruens videtur primordia ejus aperire,; cf.: congruens crediderim recensere,. —With ut: congruens est, ut, etc.,; .—
Agreeing in all its parts; symmetrical, proportioned; accordant, consistent, harmonious: is concentus ex dissimillumarum vocum moderatione concors tamen efficitur et congruens,

: Tiberius corpore fuit amplo et robusto ... ceteris quoque membris usque ad imos pedes aequalis et congruens,: congruens clamor (opp. dissonus),; cf.: congruentissimā voce acclamare,.—Hence, congrŭenter, adv., agreeably, fitly, suitably (twice in Cic., but very rare in the class. per.): congruenter naturae convenienterque vivere,: ut ad id quodcumque agetur apte congruenterque dicamus,: respondere,—Comp., ; —Sup., ;

la:adj:congruentior.gloss: uniting, combining, running or meeting together with someone

la:adj:congruus.html:
congrŭus, a, um, adj.
congruo, II.
,
agreeing, fit, suitable; harmonious, concordant (ante-, and more freq. post-class., for the class. congruens): sermo cum illā, * : sententia verecundiae maternae,: humanae naturae congruum est,: modus,: tempora,: congruo cunctae multitudinis consensu,—Adv.: con-grŭē, suitably, fitly: congrue respondere,; .

la:verb:congrego.html:
con-grĕgo, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. a., to collect into a flock or herd, to assemble.
Prop. (rare; mostly in Pliny the elder): oves,.—Mid.: apium examina congregantur,collect in swarms,; cf. : cetera animantia congregari videmus, § 5: cum ceteris,: in loca certa,: se ad amnes (ferae),.—More freq. (in good prose; esp. freq. in Cic.),
In gen., to collect or assemble a multitude together, to unite, join, associate.
Lit.: dissipatos homines,; cf.: dispersos homines in unum locum,: se unum in locum ad curiam,: dissipatos (homines) unum in locum,: multitudinem fugitivorum unum in locum,; : hominem in idem Vettii indicium atque in eundem hunc numerum,.—With cum: se cum aequalibus,; ; —With dat.: cum illis moror quibus me tempus aliquod congregavit,.—Absol.: deterrimum quemque,—Mid.: secedant improbi, unum in locum congregentur,: in fano congregantur commentandi causā,: in Academiā congregati,: armati locis patentibus congregantur,: congregabantur undique ad Titum Tatium,: quanta vis oriens et congregata,: Gamphasantes nulli externo congregantur,: ciconiae abiturae congregantur in certo loco,: cuncti deinde ad portum congregantur,: inter se,: in urbe,. —And in tmesis: conque gregantur,.—Prov.: pares cum paribus facillime congregantur,.—
Trop. (rare; mostly in Quint.), to collect, accumulate: argumenta infirmiora,: verba,; cf. turbam (verborum),; cf. congregatio, II.

germen
,
from the same stalk or stock: spicae ceteris congerminales, , 5, 7.

la:noun:congregatio.html:
congrĕgātĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
,
an assembling together; union, society, association (in good prose).
Lit.: nos ad conjunctionem congregationemque hominum et ad naturalem communitatem esse natos,; ; cf. ; Cod. Th. 18, 14, 4 al.—
Trop.: argumentorum (corresp. with colligere),: criminum (opp. separatio),: rerum (with repetitio, Gr. ἀνακεφαλαίωσις), a recapitulating, : personarum, locorum, temporum,.

con-gaudeo, ēre,

congĕrĭes, ēi (congĕrĭa, ae, and 125 Goes.; Innoc. Cas. Litt. p. 224 ib.), f.
congero

that which is brought together; hence, a heap, pile, mass (not ante-Aug.; while the syn. acervus is prevalent through all periods).
Lit.
With gen.: lapidum,: summa silvae,; cf. struis,; and: ramorum et fruticum,: cadaverum,; : densa grani,: armorum,: vasta metalli,: alta sordium,: pulveris exigui,—
Absol.: dispositam Congeriem secuit,i. e. chaos,; cf. .—So of a heap of wood, wood-pile, funeral-pile, ; ; .—

In gen.: venit aetas omnis in unam congeriem,: sincera bonorum,. —

senses: of the same herd or flock

con-grex, grĕgis, adj. (post-class.).
Of the same herd or flock: equinis armentis,: aves, dub. (al. congregatae).—Hence,
In gen., collected in flocks or multitudes: catervas, Auct. Pervig. Ven. 43: vulgo,.—With dat.: comessationibus,.—

To beget or produce at the same time (very rare; perh. only in the foll. exs., and only in the perf. part.): porci congenerati,of the same litter,; so in part.: senium parentis,.—Trop.: congeneratum verbum,of the same root,.—
To unite by affinity, to connect, Att. ap. (Trag. Rel. v. 580 Rib.).

la:verb:conglobo.html:
con-glŏbo, āvi, ātum, 1,
v a., to gather into a ball, to make spherical, to conglobate (in good prose).
Prop., constr. usu. absol., or with in and acc.; rarely with in and abl.: mare medium locum expetens conglobatur undique aequabiliter,: hic (prester) rate funditur, illud (fulmen) conglobatur impetu,; App. de Mundo, p. 62, 2.— More freq. in part. perf.: terra ipsa in sese nutibus suis conglobata,. 39, 98; so, astra nisu suo,: figura,: sanguis,: homo in semet,.—And in tmesis: corpuscula complexa inter se conque globata, * .—Hence,
In gen., to press together in a mass, to crowd together: apes, ut uvae, aliae ex aliis pendent conglobatae,: conglobato corpore in pilae modum,: homo in semet conglobatus,.— Freq., in the historians, of the collecting or crowding together of soldiers: uti quosque fors conglobaverat,; so, eos Agathyrnam,: se in unum,; cf. : in ultimam castrorum partem,: in forum,: templum in quo se miles conglobaverat,: pulsi ac fugā conglobati,; .—Absol.: fors conglobabat (sc. milites),. —Also of the elephant: conglobatae beluae,.—*
Trop.: definitiones conglobatae,heaped together, accumulated,.

,

con-glūtĭno, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. a., to glue, cement, join together.
Lit. (t. t.): favos extremos inter se,; cf.: utrasque res inter se (calx),: libros,: carnis,: volnera recentia,: germinantis oculos aliquā sibi annexione,.—
Trop.
To join, unite firmly together, to bind closely, cement (a favorite trope of Cic.; elsewhere very rare): hominem eadem, optime quae conglutinavit, natura dissolvit,; cf.: rem dissolutam, divulsamque (sc. in oratione),: animi vitium cum causā peccati,: amicitias, (opp. dissolvere); : concordiam,: voluntates nostras consuetudine,; cf.: meretricios amores nuptiis, * : quid est in Antonio praeter libidinem, crudelitatem, petulantiam, audaciam? Ex his totus conglutinatus est,composed,: affixus et conglutinatus, i. e. adhering closely to a person, .—*
Like compono, comparo, etc., to invent, devise, contrive (a means): conglutina, Ut senem hodie doctum docte fallas,.

la:verb:congelo.html:
con-gĕlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n.
Act., to cause to freeze up, to congeal.
Lit.: sal,: oleum,; : pruinas,: radices,: mare congelatum,the sea being frozen,: congelati gutta nasi,.—
Transf., to thicken, make hard: lac,to curdle,: in lapidem rictus serpentis,: ubi se adeps congelaverit,.—Humorously: quid prodest, si te congelat uxor anus?.—

Lit.: Ister congelat, .—
